I need to say something that has been weighing heavily on me lately.

I work as an RN in recovery and spend a lot of my time working on prior authorizations for people receiving substance use disorder treatment. And honestly, I’m getting tired of being told “no” when I know there is a real person on the other side of that decision who needs these services.

I understand that healthcare has guidelines, policies, criteria, and financial limitations. But sometimes I wish the people making these decisions could sit beside us for a day and see the people we see.

These are not numbers on a screen.

They are mothers and fathers. Sons and daughters. People trying to rebuild their lives after addiction has taken so much from them. They are people who are showing up, doing the work, asking for help, and trying to become the person they want to be.

My team sees them every day. We know their stories. We celebrate their accomplishments. We see their setbacks. We answer the phone when they are struggling. We watch them get jobs, repair relationships, find housing, regain their independence, and start believing in themselves again.

So when a medically necessary service is denied, it isn't just a box that gets checked or a claim that gets rejected for us. We have to look that person in the eyes and figure out how to tell them that the help they need may not be approved.

And it is heartbreaking.

I love what I do. I am passionate about recovery, mental health, and the people we serve. But I would be lying if I said it doesn't contribute to burnout. It is exhausting to fight over and over for services that we know can make a difference.

I wish we could remember that healthcare is supposed to be about PEOPLE.

Not numbers.
Not diagnoses.
Not authorization codes.
Not profit margins.

People.

Every person struggling with substance use disorder deserves to be treated like a human being whose life has value and whose recovery matters.

The people doing this work are tired. We are tired of fighting systems instead of being able to focus all of our energy on helping the people in front of us.

And yet we keep showing up.

Because they matter to us.

Their lives matter. Their recovery matters. Their future matters.

And I just wish the system could see them the way we do.

🩺 CASE MANAGER TIP OF THE DAY

📋 YOUR INSURANCE SAYS YOU NEED A PRIOR AUTHORIZATION. WHAT DOES THAT ACTUALLY MEAN?

You go to fill a prescription, schedule a test, get medical equipment, or start a treatment and suddenly hear:

“Your insurance requires prior authorization.”

First, this does NOT automatically mean your insurance denied the treatment.

A prior authorization, often called a PA, means your insurance company requires certain information and approval before it will cover a particular medication, service, procedure, or piece of equipment.

And sometimes the process gets complicated.

🔎 WHY WOULD INSURANCE REQUIRE ONE?

Your insurance plan may want documentation showing that:

✔️ The treatment is medically necessary
✔️ You meet specific coverage criteria
✔️ Other treatments have already been tried
✔️ The requested dose or frequency meets their criteria
✔️ The service is being provided appropriately under your benefits

📞 IF YOUR PA IS DELAYED, START ASKING QUESTIONS

Don't just wait indefinitely.

Call your provider and ask:

“Has the prior authorization actually been submitted?”

Then call your insurance company and ask:

“Have you received it?”

Those are TWO different questions.

A provider may believe paperwork was sent while the insurance company says it never arrived.

📋 IF IT WAS DENIED, ASK WHY

Don't stop at:

“Insurance denied it.”

Ask for the specific reason.

Was it because:

❌ Medical necessity wasn't demonstrated?
📄 Documentation was missing?
💊 Another medication must be tried first?
🏥 A different provider or facility must be used?
📋 You didn't meet the plan's coverage criteria?
💊 The medication isn't preferred on the formulary?
⏰ Something wasn't submitted within the required timeframe?

The reason for the denial determines your next step.

📝 ASK ABOUT AN APPEAL

Ask your insurance company:

“Can this decision be appealed?”

Then find out:

📅 The deadline
📄 What documentation is needed
👩‍⚕️ What your provider needs to submit
📞 Where the appeal should be sent
⏰ How long the review may take
🚨 Whether an expedited review is available when medically appropriate

Sometimes your healthcare provider can provide additional records or a more detailed explanation of why the requested treatment is medically necessary.

👩‍⚕️ ASK WHETHER A PEER-TO-PEER REVIEW IS AN OPTION

Depending on the situation and insurance plan, your provider may be able to discuss the request directly with a clinician reviewing the case.

Ask:

“Is a peer-to-peer review available for this denial?”

Not every denial qualifies, but it is worth asking.

💊 SOMETIMES INSURANCE WANTS YOU TO TRY SOMETHING ELSE FIRST

This is sometimes called step therapy.

The plan may require you to try a preferred medication or treatment before it will cover another option.

If you've already tried it, couldn't tolerate it, had a reaction, or it didn't work:

MAKE SURE YOUR PROVIDER DOCUMENTS THAT.

Your medical record matters.

🗂️ KEEP A PAPER TRAIL

Write down:

📅 Dates
☎️ Phone numbers
👤 Names or departments
🔢 Reference numbers
📋 Authorization numbers
❌ Denial reasons
⏰ Deadlines
📝 What each person tells you

And keep copies of denial letters.

You may need that information later.

💡 CASE MANAGER TIP:

When you hear:

“Your prior authorization was denied.”

Your next question should NOT simply be:

“How much will it cost me?”

Your next question should be:

“WHY was it denied, and what is the next step?”

Then ask:

➡️ Can additional documentation be submitted?
➡️ Can it be appealed?
➡️ Is peer-to-peer review available?
➡️ Is there a covered alternative?
➡️ Is there an expedited process if medically necessary?

❤️ A DENIAL IS A DECISION BASED ON YOUR INSURANCE PLAN'S COVERAGE RULES.

It is not automatically the same thing as your doctor saying:

“You don't need this.”

Learn the reason.

Know your options.

Keep records.

Ask questions.

And advocate for yourself.

Sometimes navigating healthcare requires persistence, and knowing what to ask next can make all the difference. 🩺📋

I rarely post explicitly about this disease, but having been diagnosed with M.E. myself just a few weeks ago after 4 years now of battling symptoms - there is no end in sight. Quality of life is ranked lower than end-stage diseases, and giving up your autonomy to this chronic illness can make anyone want to give up. I’m hopeful medicine catches up, and I will continue to push until I physically can’t. The hardest part besides the brain fog, murderous fatigue and joint pains is watching my body whither away. Stretch marks replace where muscle was. Having set an amateur deadlift record to now struggling to chase my dog. I don’t post about “being sick” much, but damn this changed me from living life to pushing through it. I just started with a new doctor in the field… we’ll see, yet again.

🏥 Common Medical Billing Denial Codes

A denied claim is not the end of the billing process. It is an opportunity to identify the root cause, correct the issue, and prevent the same denial from happening again.

Here are some common Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARCs) that medical billing professionals should understand:

🔹 Patient Information Errors

CO-31: Patient cannot be identified as the insured
CO-9: Diagnosis is inconsistent with the patient's age
CO-16: Claim/service lacks information or has a billing error

🔹 Insurance Coverage Issues

CO-22: Care may be covered by another payer due to coordination of benefits
CO-26: Expenses incurred prior to coverage
CO-27: Expenses incurred after coverage terminated

🔹 Authorization & Referral Issues

CO-15: Authorization number is missing, invalid, or does not apply
CO-197: Precertification/authorization/notification was absent
CO-252: Required attachment or supporting documentation is missing

🔹 Medical Necessity & Coding Issues

CO-50: Services are not considered medically necessary by the payer
CO-11: Diagnosis is inconsistent with the procedure
CO-49: Service is non-covered because it is a routine/preventive or screening service

💡 The key to effective denial management is not simply reworking a denied claim — it's understanding WHY the claim was denied.

Accurate patient information, eligibility verification, authorization checks, proper coding, complete documentation, and timely follow-up can help reduce avoidable denials and improve the overall revenue cycle.

Know the code. Identify the cause. Fix the gap. Prevent the next denial.

He was talking about my son, Cole.

When I heard these words, I immediately thought about January 2024.

Cole needed medication that could help keep him alive. He couldn’t afford it after his prescription coverage changed, and the system failed him.

He died on January 21, 2024.

So when someone says, “our current health system still forces people to walk away from medicine that will literally keep them alive because they can’t fucking afford it,” I don’t hear a talking point.

I hear my son’s story.

This is why I keep fighting for PBM reform.

Because behind every denied prescription, every formulary change, every prior authorization and every unaffordable copay is a real person.

Sometimes, that person is someone’s son.

His name was Cole.

#PBMReform #ColeSchmidtknecht #Healthcare #PatientsFirst

Prior authorization (also called pre-approval) means your health plan requires you to get approval before it will cover certain services, treatments, or prescriptions. 

If you skip this step, you might be stuck paying the full cost out of pocket—even if it’s a service normally covered. 😬

✅ Used to confirm medical necessity
✅ Helps prevent unnecessary or overly expensive treatments
✅ Common in Medicare Advantage & private plans

Not sure if a procedure, test, or prescription needs pre-approval? Look in your plan’s Summary of Benefits or EOC, or log in to your member portal to check documentation. 

When in doubt, call the insurance provider or even your doctor's office. They should know because they often submit it for you. Make sure you know or you could end up paying out of pocket. Need help reviewing your plan? We’re just a message away! 💬

Then Dad texted: """"If you don't, you're not welcome for Thanksgiving. My sister also sent: """"I already told my landlord you'd wire it today. Don't make me look stupid.""""I sent one reply to all of them: """"Good luck."""" By the weekend, their landlord called me - and now my sister's stuff is on the curb, Mom's crying, and Dad is texting: """"What did you say to him?! He's evicting her today! Answer your phone now!!!""""
My sister called while I was standing in the frozen food aisle holding a bag of peas.
No hello. No buildup. No pretense.
“You’re paying my rent this month,” she said. “Twenty-six hundred. Dad says you make more, so shut up and help.”
I stood there under the white grocery store lights, one hand on the cart, and actually looked around to make sure I had heard correctly. A little kid was begging his mother for cereal at the endcap. Somewhere behind me, a cashier laughed. Life was continuing normally while my family, once again, treated my bank account like a utility they were entitled to access.
“Excuse me?” I said.
My younger sister, Brianna, huffed like I was the difficult one. “I already told my landlord you’d wire it today. Don’t make me look stupid.”
That line almost made me laugh.
Almost.
Brianna was twenty-nine, beautiful, dramatic, and permanently one bad decision ahead of a crisis. There was always a reason she needed money right now. First it was a car payment, then a “temporary” medical bill that turned out to be cosmetic dental work, then a security deposit, then credit cards, then a “business idea” involving a mobile spray-tan service she ran for four months before deciding she hated customers. My parents never stopped rescuing her. They just started needing my money to do it.
Before I could answer, another text lit up my phone.
From my father.
If you don’t help, you’re not welcome for Thanksgiving.
That was three days away.
I stared at the message and felt something go cold and perfectly still inside me.
Because it wasn’t just manipulation anymore. It was extortion dressed up as family loyalty. Pay your sister’s rent or lose your place at the table. Transfer money or be cast as the selfish daughter who abandoned everyone over “one little favor.”
My mother, of course, said nothing herself. She never had to. She let my father issue the threats and Brianna make the demands while she played peacemaker afterward, crying about family unity and how hard things had been for everyone.
I checked out without buying half the groceries in my cart. By the time I reached my car, Brianna had sent two more texts.
Landlord wants it by 5.
Don’t embarrass me.
I sat behind the wheel and closed my eyes for one long second.
For years, I had paid. Not every time, but enough. I was thirty-five, a CPA in Raleigh, North Carolina, with a stable income, a condo I actually owned, and a life built on the kind of planning my family found useful only when it benefited them. I paid for Brianna’s moving truck when she got dumped and had to leave an apartment overnight. I covered her car insurance once because “it was easier than letting her lose the vehicle.” I even paid off a utility shutoff notice last winter after my mother called crying and said, “She just needs one good month to get back on her feet.”
There was never one good month.
Only the next emergency.
This time, though, something felt different. Not because the amount was bigger. Because of the arrogance. The certainty. Brianna had already promised my money to another adult before even asking me. My father had backed her up with a holiday threat. Neither of them seemed to believe I had any choice.
So I sent one reply to the group thread.
Good luck.
Then I silenced my phone and drove home.
By the weekend, their landlord called me directly.
And by then, my sister’s furniture was already on the curb, my mother was sobbing, and my father was texting in all caps asking what I had said to him.
The answer was simple.Nothing they were going to like...I did not contact the landlord first.
That was the part my father kept getting wrong in his messages, as if I had somehow orchestrated the entire collapse by making one vindictive call from my car in the grocery store parking lot.
I hadn’t.
My sister had done that all by herself.
The landlord called me Saturday morning at 8:26 because Brianna had listed me as her emergency financial contact on the original lease application—without my permission. I found that out when a man named Thomas Heller introduced himself in a clipped, tired voice and asked, “Ms. Mercer, are you aware that your sister represented you as guarantor-adjacent support for this tenancy?”
I was making coffee when he called. I set the mug down slowly. “No,” I said. “I did not agree to guarantee anything.” He exhaled, not surprised. “That is what I suspected.” Then he explained the situation.
Brianna had not simply fallen short on one month’s rent. She was already behind. The twenty-six hundred she demanded from me was not a one-time gap; it was the final amount due after prior late balances, fees, and a failed payment arrangement. She had told Mr. Heller that her “high-earning sister” would wire the full amount Friday, which bought her an extra twenty-four hours she had no right to promise. When no payment arrived, he posted final possession notice and began legal turnover on the unit because the lease was already in default.
That was bad enough. Then he added the detail that changed everything. “She also told me,” he said, “that if I had concerns, I could speak directly with your father because he was handling family money.”
Of course she had.
I leaned against the kitchen counter and felt the old family system unfolding in perfect, ugly shape. Brianna lied. Dad amplified it. Mom cried. Then everyone acted shocked when reality refused to cooperate.
“What exactly do you need from me?” I asked. “Nothing financial,” Mr. Heller said. “I need clarity. Are you legally involved in this lease or not?” “No.”
“Did you authorize your sister to represent that you would pay?” “No.” There was a pause. I could hear papers moving on his end. “Thank you,” he said. “I needed that on record.”
That sentence explained the rest.
Thomas Heller wasn’t evicting Brianna because of something I said. He was moving forward because the one thing still keeping her afloat—my presumed money—had just disappeared officially. She had used my name as a bluff, and he had called it.
My father started texting half an hour later.
What did you tell him?!
He says you denied helping her!
Her stuff is on the curb!
Answer your phone NOW!!!
I didn’t answer immediately. I made breakfast. I sat at my kitchen island. I ate scrambled eggs while my phone lit up with the kind of panic my family usually reserved for moments when consequences stopped being theoretical.
Then my mother called. I answered her because I already knew what she would sound like: breathless, shaking, deeply invested in the idea that I could still reverse everything if I stopped being “difficult.”
“Lena,” she cried, “please tell me this is a misunderstanding.” “No,” I said. “She said you spoke to the landlord.”
“I did. He called me.” “He’s putting her things outside!” “That means she was already out of options.” My mother made a small broken sound. “How can you be so cold?”
I looked around my quiet kitchen, at the bills I paid on time, the order I had built for myself, the peace that always seemed to feel insulting to them whenever Brianna’s life was on fire. “I’m not cold,” I said. “I’m not lying for her anymore.” That line stopped her for a second.
Then came my father in the background, loud enough to hear through the phone. “Ask her what she told him!” I answered him without needing him on the line.
“I told him the truth. That I’m not on the lease, I never promised payment, and Brianna used my name without permission.” My mother whispered, horrified, “Why would you do that?” Because I was tired.
Because this is how adults sink—one false emergency at a time, with the most responsible person in the room expected to serve as the floor beneath everyone else’s poor choices.
But what I said was simpler. “Because it’s true.” The screaming started after that. Not from me. From them.
And once my father finally got on the phone himself, he made one mistake that ended any chance of this becoming a private family argument. He threatened me.READ THE FULL STORY below 👇"

I was thirty-five, a CPA in Raleigh, North Carolina, with a stable income, a condo I actually owned, and a life built on the kind of planning my family found useful only when it benefited them. I paid for Brianna’s moving truck when she got dumped and had to leave an apartment overnight. I covered her car insurance once because “it was easier than letting her lose the vehicle.” I even paid off a utility shutoff notice last winter after my mother called crying and said, “She just needs one good month to get back on her feet.”
There was never one good month.
Only the next emergency.
This time, though, something felt different. Not because the amount was bigger. Because of the arrogance. The certainty. Brianna had already promised my money to another adult before even asking me. My father had backed her up with a holiday threat. Neither of them seemed to believe I had any choice.
So I sent one reply to the group thread.
Good luck.

By the weekend, their landlord called me directly.

The answer was simple.Nothing they were going to like...I did not contact the landlord first.
That was the part my father kept getting wrong in his messages, as if I had somehow orchestrated the entire collapse by making one vindictive call from my car in the grocery store parking lot.
I hadn’t.
My sister had done that all by herself.

I found that out when a man named Thomas Heller introduced himself in a clipped, tired voice and asked, “Ms. Mercer, are you aware that your sister represented you as guarantor-adjacent support for this tenancy?”

The twenty-six hundred she demanded from me was not a one-time gap; it was the final amount due after prior late balances, fees, and a failed payment arrangement. She had told Mr. Heller that her “high-earning sister” would wire the full amount Friday, which bought her an extra twenty-four hours she had no right to promise. When no payment arrived, he posted final possession notice and began legal turnover on the unit because the lease was already in default.
That was bad enough. Then he added the detail that changed everything. “She also told me,” he said, “that if I had concerns, I could speak directly with your father because he was handling family money.”
Of course she had.

“What exactly do you need from me?” I asked. “Nothing financial,” Mr. Heller said. “I need clarity. Are you legally involved in this lease or not?” “No.”

That sentence explained the rest.
Thomas Heller wasn’t evicting Brianna because of something I said. He was moving forward because the one thing still keeping her afloat—my presumed money—had just disappeared officially. She had used my name as a bluff, and he had called it.

What did you tell him?!
He says you denied helping her!
Her stuff is on the curb!
Answer your phone NOW!!!

Then my mother called. I answered her because I already knew what she would sound like: breathless, shaking, deeply invested in the idea that I could still reverse everything if I stopped being “difficult.”
“Lena,” she cried, “please tell me this is a misunderstanding.” “No,” I said. “She said you spoke to the landlord.”
“I did. He called me.” “He’s putting her things outside!” “That means she was already out of options.” My mother made a small broken sound. “How can you be so cold?”
I looked around my quiet kitchen, at the bills I paid on time, the order I had built for myself, the peace that always seemed to feel insulting to them whenever Brianna’s life was on fire. “I’m not cold,” I said. “I’m not lying for her anymore.” That line stopped her for a second.
Then came my father in the background, loud enough to hear through the phone. “Ask her what she told him!” I answered him without needing him on the line.
“I told him the truth. That I’m not on the lease, I never promised payment, and Brianna used my name without permission.” My mother whispered, horrified, “Why would you do that?” Because I was tired.
Because this is how adults sink—one false emergency at a time, with the most responsible person in the room expected to serve as the floor beneath everyone else’s poor choices.
But what I said was simpler. “Because it’s true.” The screaming started after that. Not from me. From them.

WHY ARE WE DOING THIS?

Because we have seen too much.

We have watched people go without medications they need because they simply cannot afford them.

We have worked in a healthcare system where providers can be expected to see patient after patient in 15-minute appointments — while the person sitting across from us may have a lifetime of medical problems, questions, fears and a story that cannot possibly fit into 15 minutes.

We have watched tests get delayed. Prior authorizations get denied. Medications become unaffordable. Patients fall through cracks that seem to get wider every year.

Meanwhile, chronic disease continues to get worse.

At some point, we had to ask ourselves:

What if we stopped waiting for healthcare to change and started doing our small part differently?

What if we went to the patient?

What if we removed the cost of the visit?

What if we had time to listen?

What if we looked beyond the diagnosis and saw the whole person sitting in front of us?

What if healthcare could feel like caring for people again?

That is why Twisted Roots Medical Mission exists.

We don't believe one mobile medical mission can fix everything that is wrong with healthcare.

But we can make a difference for the person sitting in front of us.

We can check the blood pressure.

We can find the diabetes that hasn't been diagnosed.

We can help someone figure out how to get the medication they haven't been able to afford.

We can listen to the story.

We can treat people with dignity.

And when transportation, finances, geography or life itself keeps someone from getting to healthcare—

we can take healthcare to them.

Our faith is part of what brought us here. But this mission is about something every person deserves, regardless of background or belief:

Excellent healthcare. Compassion. Dignity. And the knowledge that someone actually cares what happens to you.

That's why we're building Twisted Roots Medical Mission.

🌿 Care that reaches. Hope that lasts.

Here’s a quick case for the advocates in this group/feed.

A client calls and says:
“My insurance won’t approve my treatment.”
The physician’s office tells her:
“We’re waiting on insurance.”
She believes she needs help getting the prior authorization approved.

What’s your first move?
Do you immediately start chasing the authorization?
Or do you first determine whether prior authorization is actually the thing preventing treatment from moving forward?

Because those are not necessarily the same problem.

Maybe it’s coverage.
Maybe it’s medical-necessity criteria.
Maybe it’s network.
Maybe documentation is missing.
Maybe another utilization rule applies.
Maybe the treatment is ready but the patient can’t afford their portion.
Or maybe everyone involved thinks somebody else owns the next step.

This is why I think treatment-access work requires something more valuable than administrative follow-up:
diagnosis of the barrier.

If this were your client, what would you investigate first?

A quick update for my hypermobility/Ehlers-Danlos patients regarding genetic testing:

Unfortunately, getting genetic testing authorized through insurance has become increasingly difficult. Many insurance companies now require additional prior-authorization paperwork, and coverage requirements can vary significantly from one plan to another.

The biggest concern is cost. If testing is not authorized by your insurance and financial arrangements are not confirmed with the laboratory ahead of time, genetic testing can potentially cost up to $5,000. In the past, I was able to ensure patients access testing for around $250 when insurance denied coverage. Unfortunately, that option is no longer available.

Before proceeding with genetic testing, I recommend:
• Contacting your insurance company to ask which genetic testing laboratories are preferred or in-network with your plan.
• Asking whether your plan requires testing to be ordered or authorized by a geneticist, genetic counselor, or another specific type of provider that is in network.
• Confirming your out-of-pocket cost directly with the laboratory before your sample is collected or testing is performed.
• Exploring reputable and affordable self-pay/direct-to-consumer genetic testing options when appropriate.

A note about direct-to-consumer genetic testing: I do not have any financial relationships or affiliations with genetic testing companies, and I do not endorse a specific company or panel. Different companies test for different genes and variants, and the way results are reported can vary considerably. These reports can be confusing—especially when they include variants whose clinical significance is uncertain.

If you choose to obtain genetic testing on your own, you are welcome to bring your results to your appointment. I am happy to review the panel with you and help interpret it within the limits of my knowledge and expertise. When appropriate, additional interpretation by a geneticist or genetic counselor may still be helpful.

Please also remember that genetic testing is only one piece of the puzzle. A negative genetic test does not rule out hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), because there is currently no established molecular genetic test that confirms hEDS.

My goal is to help you get the testing you need while avoiding an unexpected bill—and unfortunately, that now requires a little more homework for patients and a lot of time consuming paperwork for me before sending the test.
